sections.h2: What is Mahaska County, Iowa, like as a place to own a house?
sections.html:
Mahaska County is a south-central Iowa county of about 573 square miles, nearly all of it land, with 22,190 residents in 2020. Oskaloosa is the seat and the biggest city, at 11,558 people.

Its neighbors are Jasper, Poweshiek, Keokuk, Wapello, Monroe and Marion counties. The population has barely moved since 1980,, which means a stable base of owners and few sudden swings in headcount. Beyond Oskaloosa, the larger places are New Sharon (1,262), Eddyville (970) and Fremont (708), with smaller communities such as Beacon and University Park.

sections.h2: How did coal and the county seat shape Mahaska County?
sections.html:
Mahaska County was formed in 1843, named for Chief Mahaska of the Iowa people, and began governing itself in 1844. Coal mining was once a leading industry, and by 1895 the county out-produced every other Iowa county in coal.

The Muchakinock coal camp near Oskaloosa was among the largest in Iowa in the 1800s, and a 1902 explosion at the Lost Creek No. 2 mine killed 20 men. Oskaloosa was platted and named county seat in 1844 and incorporated in 1875. Its courthouse, finished in 1886 and designed by Henry C. Koch, is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Deeds and parcel records for old mining ground are kept at the courthouse, so a seller with a rural parcel can look them up there.

sections.h2: What does the Mahaska County economy look like?
sections.html:
Oskaloosa's economy rests on sports lighting, healthcare, education, manufacturing and retail. Musco Lighting and Mahaska Health Partnership appear among the larger employers named in an older survey cited on Wikipedia, alongside Oskaloosa Community Schools, Clow Valve Company and William Penn University.

William Penn University was founded by Quakers in 1873 as Penn College, took the William Penn College name in 1933 and became a university in 2000. The headcounts in that survey date from 2010, so treat them as background only.

  • Oskaloosa lies between the Skunk and Des Moines rivers, at about 846 feet.
  • Lake Keomah State Park is roughly four miles east of town.
  • Climate normals for 1991 to 2020 show about 38.7 inches of precipitation and 25.1 inches of snow a year, with a July average high near 85.5 degrees.

Those winters and summers are why roofs, furnaces and gutters are the first things a buyer's inspector checks.

sections.h2: Which Mahaska County offices deal with property tax?
sections.html:
The Assessor and the Treasurer both operate from the Mahaska County Courthouse at 106 South 1st Street in Oskaloosa. The Assessor sets value, the Treasurer collects.

OfficeContactHours
Assessor, Lindsey Thomas(641) 673-5805, thomas@mahaskacountyia.gov8:00 am to 4:30 pm, Monday to Friday
Treasurer, property tax(641) 673-5482, treasurer@mahaskacountyia.gov8:00 am to 4:30 pm, Monday to Friday

The Assessor page offers Beacon maps and records, a sales report and a Data Correction Form you reach from any parcel report. If a house has a new addition or lost a building, owners can email the office with the address and a phone number.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Mahaska County property value?
sections.html:
Start by looking at your parcel in Beacon, then ask the Assessor to review it informally between April 2 and April 25, or file a written protest by April 30. The Mahaska Assessor page does not list protest dates, so these come from state rules in Iowa Code 441.37 and the Department of Revenue.

Written protests go on the state form and the signer is the owner or an agent. The statute lets a board allow electronic filing, and it allows owners to correct clerical or mathematical errors going back to earlier years if those years are not fully paid.

  • Treat the January 1 value as the target: that is the date assessments reflect.
  • Bring recent nearby sales if you argue the value is too high.
  • If you say the house is in the wrong class, bring proof of how it is used.

sections.h2: What happens after a protest in Mahaska County?
sections.html:
The local board of review hears protests starting May 1 and has until May 31 to finish unless the state grants an extension, which cannot run past July 15. A written decision must be mailed no later than three days after adjournment.

An owner who still disagrees may go to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court, with 20 days counted from adjournment or May 31, whichever is later. The board's members serve six-year staggered terms, and at least one must be a farmer, according to the Iowa Department of Revenue.

sections.h2: When does Mahaska County property tax become delinquent?
sections.html:
The first half goes delinquent October 1 and the second half April 1, under Iowa Code chapter 445. A late half carries interest of one and one-half percent for each month or part of a month.

Interest is rounded to the nearest whole dollar with a floor of $1. You can pay online through the Iowa Treasurers' parcel search, in person at the courthouse or by mail to 106 S 1st Street. The Treasurer's page does not post due dates, so ask the office at (641) 673-5482 for the amounts on your parcel before closing.

sections.h2: How does the Mahaska County tax sale work?
sections.html:
Iowa treasurers offer delinquent parcels each June, normally on the third Monday, and the buyer pays the taxes, interest, fees and costs. The owner can redeem later by paying the sale price, a certificate fee and 2% interest per month, per Iowa Code 446.7 and 447.1.

Mahaska's Treasurer page does not describe a sale, and the Sheriff Sale link on that site is a different office and a different process. If you inherited a house with back taxes, check the parcel with the Treasurer first.

sections.h2: What does selling a Mahaska County house cost in taxes and filings?
sections.html:
Iowa charges transfer tax at 80 cents for each $500 above the first $500 of value. A declaration of value goes in with the deed, and the recorder sends it to the assessor, who keeps it for three years (Iowa Code 428A.1).

The Iowa homestead credit matters for the closing date. A new owner of a house that sold before July 1 has to claim the credit by July 1, while a sale on or after July 1 leaves the credit with the property for that year, under rule 701-110.1.

  • Taxes are a lien on the parcel against everyone except the state.
  • A refund claim for tax paid in error must be made within two years of the due date.
  • The treasurer's receipt showing full payment is conclusive proof the parcel was free of taxes.

sections.h2: What should a Mahaska County owner do before listing?
sections.html:
Gather three things first: a payoff statement, the parcel record and any repair or damage list. Those let you compare what you owe against what the house can sell for.

  • Pull the Beacon parcel report and use the Data Correction Form for wrong details.
  • Call the Treasurer for the current amount, interest included.
  • If the house is an inheritance, confirm which owners are of record at the courthouse.
  • Note whether the Assessor has a homestead credit on file and tell the buyer.

faqs.q: Where is the Mahaska County Assessor's office?
faqs.a: It is on the first floor of the Mahaska County Courthouse, 106 South 1st Street, Oskaloosa, IA 52577, in the southeast corner. Phone is (641) 673-5805, open weekdays 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

faqs.q: What is the property tax protest window in Mahaska County?
faqs.a: April 2 through April 30, set by state law. An informal review with the Assessor runs April 2 through April 25.

faqs.q: How can I pay Mahaska County property tax?
faqs.a: Online through the Iowa Treasurers' parcel search, in person at the courthouse on weekdays, or by mail to 106 S 1st Street. The property tax line is (641) 673-5482.

faqs.q: How much is the late fee on Iowa property tax?
faqs.a: Interest is one and one-half percent per month, rounded to the nearest dollar, with a $1 minimum. A partial month counts as a full month.

faqs.q: Is Oskaloosa the biggest city in Mahaska County?
faqs.a: Yes. Oskaloosa had 11,558 residents in 2020 and is the county seat.
